title: Butterflies: Caterpillars with Wings!
summary: Part two of a two-part series on insects, focusing on butterflies. The hosts cover how butterflies differ from moths (diurnal vs. nocturnal), the origin of the word "butterfly," butterfly anatomy (eyes, antennae, labial palps, proboscis, legs, wings), emergence from the chrysalis and wing inflation, thermoregulation and basking, monarch migration and the Mexico logging crisis, feeding habits (puddling, fruit, minerals), mating and spermatophores, host-plant relationships, threats from pesticides, roads, and collecting, and how to plant a butterfly garden with native plants (including the invasive butterfly bush and tropical milkweed concerns). They close with a note on Rh blood factor research inspired by butterfly mimicry, followed by listener mail about Spotify search associations.

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce final three live shows of the year in Orlando, Nashville, and Atlanta, with ticket info on the website.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as part two on insects, reference the caterpillar episode, and thank HowStuffWorks writers Tracy Wilson and Jennifer Horton.

segments.title: Butterflies vs. moths and emergence from chrysalis
segments.summary: After emerging from the chrysalis, butterflies are built for reproduction. The hosts discuss how butterflies descended from moths that became active in daytime, and why moths are attracted to light (moon navigation) while butterflies navigate by the sun.

segments.title: Etymology of the word butterfly
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Old English origin of the word, including the folk belief that butterflies stole butter and milk, reflected in German and Dutch names.

segments.title: Butterfly eyes, antennae, and labial palps
segments.summary: Butterflies have compound eyes that detect color; monarchs have about twelve thousand eyes. Antennae sense light, odors, pheromones, and wingbeats. Labial palps are thought to detect CO2 and food.

segments.title: Proboscis and legs
segments.summary: The proboscis is a tongue-like organ used for sipping nectar, and its two parts must be joined after emergence. Butterflies have six legs that taste sugar, causing the proboscis to uncoil.

segments.title: Wings and iridescence
segments.summary: The hosts reference an earlier iridescence episode. Wing scales are transparent and multilayered, the wings are made of chitin, and wing veins are species-specific and used in mate recognition.

segments.title: Wing damage and meconium after emergence
segments.summary: Butterflies cannot repair damaged wings. After emerging, they pass meconium, a red waste left from the caterpillar stage, clean their bodies, and pump fluid through wing veins to inflate and dry their wings.

segments.title: Pump-up sneakers tangent
segments.summary: The hosts compare wing inflation to 1990s pump-up basketball shoes by Reebok, which they recall were endorsed by Spud Webb.

segments.title: Cold weather and flight
segments.summary: After drying their wings, butterflies struggle to fly in cold, rain, or wind. The hosts tease the explanation of how temperature affects them after a break.

segments.title: Butterfly temperature regulation and basking
segments.summary: Butterflies are ectotherms whose muscles fail below a set temperature; they work best near 82 F (28 C). Wings are used for defense, display, and warming (basking, reflecting sun, shivering). They fold wings to limit heat. Butterflies shelter at night.

segments.title: Monarch migration and the Mexico logging crisis
segments.summary: Monarchs migrate from eastern Canada to northwest Mexico over about eight months across multiple generations. A kaleidoscope is a group of butterflies. Illegal logging in 2015 at the Butterfly Biosphere Reserve destroyed acres; migration numbers fell from a billion in 1996 to about thirty-five million in 2016, and have since risen.

segments.title: Butterfly diet, puddling, and minerals
segments.summary: Butterflies need minerals beyond nectar and get them by puddling, from dung, urine, and rotting fruit. Studies on monarchs found mashed banana fed adults laid nearly twice as many eggs. Butterfly pollination is called psychophily.

segments.title: Butterfly mating and spermatophores
segments.summary: Butterflies recognize mates with antennae and pheromones. Males deliver a spermatophore with nutrients; some males seal the female to prevent later mating. Females lay eggs before fertilization, which happens externally. Green veined white males emit a pheromone smelling like lemon oil.

segments.title: Butterfly reproduction and eggs
segments.summary: Gestation is about three days, and females lay ten to three hundred eggs over two to four weeks. Eggs need proper humidity and temperature and face predators. Many species are plant-specific, with caterpillars eating the plant they hatch on.

segments.title: Butterfly bush as invasive plant
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the butterfly bush, which provides nectar but not host support for caterpillars, is considered invasive, and can distract butterflies from native plants.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning to discuss butterfly population threats.

segments.title: Threats to butterflies: pesticides, caterpillar pest control, urbanization, roads
segments.summary: Pesticides are a major threat, and butterflies are very sensitive to them. Killing caterpillars as pests harms butterflies too. Development destroys habitat, and roadside margins attract butterflies into traffic.

segments.title: Butterfly collecting
segments.summary: Collecting butterflies for display is a practice that harms endangered species, since rarer species become more desirable. Legal protections exist but are rarely enforced. Antique specimens are legal.

segments.title: Planting a butterfly garden
segments.summary: Hosts recommend learning local butterfly species, planting native host and nectar plants, providing water puddles and rocks for basking, and avoiding pesticides. Native butterfly weed is good; tropical milkweed blooms late and can harm monarchs via protozoan parasites. Personal anecdotes about hornets and wild backyards follow.

segments.title: Rh blood factor and butterfly mimicry
segments.summary: The hosts close the factual portion by noting that butterfly mimicry inspired Sir Cyril Clark's discovery of the Rh blood factor and its role in treating hemolytic disease of the newborn.

segments.title: Listener mail: Spotify search associations
segments.summary: A listener notes that searching Owner of a Lonely Heart and Milli Vanilli on Spotify may have linked them algorithmically. The hosts run an experiment with Black Sabbath's Warpigs and Barry Manilow's Even Now, dubbed Corey's in Charge.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to email results of the experiment and close the show.
